title: Unit – 5 : Session – 2 : SLO – 2  |  Graph Representation — Adjacency List
sections: In an adjacency list, each vertex in a graph is associated with a LINKED LIST (list of its neighbours).
The adjacency list is more efficient in terms of space for SPARSE graphs.
The time complexity for checking if there is an edge between two vertices in an adjacency list is O(degree) / O(V) worst case.
In an undirected graph, if there is an edge between vertex A and vertex B, then both A and B will appear in each other's ADJACENCY LIST.
The space complexity of an adjacency list representation is O(V + E).
Adjacency list is preferred for representing dense graphs — FALSE (matrix is preferred for dense graphs).
In a directed graph, each edge is stored in both vertices' adjacency lists — FALSE (stored only at the source).
Adjacency list can store weights along with the edges in a weighted graph — TRUE.
Traversing all neighbours of a vertex in an adjacency list is faster than in an adjacency matrix for sparse graphs — TRUE.
Adjacency list: an array of linked lists; each vertex stores a list of all vertices adjacent to it.
Advantages: (1) memory efficient for sparse graphs, O(V + E) space; (2) fast iteration over a vertex's neighbours.
IV. Adjacency List — Undirected Graph (edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, B-E, D-E)
